entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To criticize someone, often in front of others, so that they feel stupid or unimportant.
entries.usage: Common in talk about relationships, families and workplaces; it describes unkind, belittling behavior: *He's always putting her down.* A pronoun must go in the middle (*put me down*), and the noun *put-down* means an insulting remark. Be careful: *put an animal down* means to kill it painlessly.
entries.pattern: put someone down (in front of others); put yourself down
examples: Her boyfriend **puts her down** in front of her friends, and it's hard to watch.
Good teachers correct mistakes without **putting kids down**.
Stop **putting yourself down** — you did a great job.

drill.sentence: My older brother used to {{put me down}} whenever I tried to join his friends' games.
drill.hint: make me feel stupid with his comments (not *make fun of me*)

entries.related: *belittle* — more formal, make someone seem unimportant; *make fun of* — laugh at someone unkindly; *talk down to* — speak to someone as if they were stupid.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To become friends again with someone after an argument or a fight.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about friends, couples and kids: *Have you made up with her yet?* Without *with*, both people are the subject: *They had a fight, but they've made up.* Don't confuse it with *make it up to someone*, which means to do something nice to repay them after you let them down.
entries.pattern: make up with someone; they made up
examples: Have you **made up with** your sister yet, or are you still not talking?
The kids fought all morning, but they **made up** by lunch.
I **made up with** my old roommate after not speaking to her for two years.

drill.sentence: After the argument, it took Lena three days to {{make up with}} her best friend.
drill.hint: become friends again with (not *patch things up with*)

entries.related: *patch things up* — repair a relationship after a fight; *make it up to someone* — do something nice to apologize; *fall out with* — the opposite, have a serious argument.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To stop taking part in an agreement, deal, event or activity, especially before it is finished.
entries.usage: Common in news and business: *pull out of a deal / a race / a tournament / a contract*. Use *of* before the thing you leave; without it, there is no object (*Two sponsors have pulled out*). It often suggests a sudden decision that causes problems for others.
entries.pattern: pull out of + a deal / a race / a tournament
examples: The tennis star **pulled out of** the tournament with a wrist injury.
Our biggest investor **pulled out** two weeks before the launch.
We had to **pull out of** the deal on the house when the inspection found mold.

drill.sentence: The singer {{pulled out of}} the festival after losing her voice, and fans got their money back.
drill.hint: withdrew from (not *backed out of*, *bowed out of* or *dropped out of*)

entries.related: *back out of* — withdraw from something you promised, often seen as unreliable; *drop out of* — leave a course or a race; *withdraw from* — formal.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To move a vehicle to the side of the road and stop it.
entries.usage: Common in driving situations, often as a request to the driver (*Can you pull over for a second?*). It is often intransitive (*The driver pulled over*), but the police can *pull someone over*, with a pronoun in the middle (*pulled me over*). Compare *pull up*, which means to stop at a particular place, such as in front of a house.
entries.pattern: pull over (at / to the side); the police pulled someone over
examples: I **pulled over** to check the map because my phone kept losing signal.
A cop **pulled me over** for going fifty in a thirty-five zone.
Can you **pull over** at the next gas station? I need a bathroom.

drill.sentence: When you hear a siren behind you, you're supposed to {{pull over}} and let the ambulance pass.
drill.hint: move to the roadside and stop

entries.related: *pull up* — stop at a particular place; *pull in* — drive into a parking space or a driveway; *pull out* — drive onto a road.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To give information, a message or something you have received to another person.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and work email: *I'll pass that along*, *pass along a message / a tip / my thanks*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*pass it along*), and *to* names the person (*pass it along to Sam*). British speakers more often say *pass on*, which Americans use too.
entries.pattern: pass along + a message / thanks (to someone); pass it along
examples: If you see Mia, can you **pass along** my congratulations?
Thanks for the feedback — I'll **pass it along** to the chef.
My coworker **passed along** the news that the office will be closed on Friday.

drill.sentence: Rachel called while you were out and asked me to {{pass along}} a message about Friday's dinner.
drill.hint: deliver to you, with the particle Americans prefer here (not *relay*)

entries.related: *pass on* — same meaning, more common in British English; *relay* — formal, pass a message between people; *forward* — send on an email or a letter.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To realize that someone is trying to trick or deceive you, or that their excuse or charm is not sincere.
entries.usage: Common in conversation: *I can see right through you*, *see through his lies / the excuse / the act*. The person or trick follows *through*, and *right* often adds emphasis. Don't confuse it with *see something through*, which means to continue until something is finished.
entries.pattern: see (right) through + someone / a lie / an act
examples: He acted friendly, but my grandmother **saw through** him right away.
Kids can **see through** fake praise faster than adults think.
Nice try, but I can **see right through** you — you just want to borrow my car.

drill.sentence: The salesman's flattery didn't work on my mom; she {{saw through}} it immediately.
drill.hint: recognized it as fake

entries.related: *fall for* — the opposite, be tricked; *read someone like a book* — understand someone's thoughts easily; *see something through* — continue until it is finished.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be completely sold, so that none are left; or, about a store, to sell all of something it has.
entries.usage: Used for tickets, products and events: *The concert sold out in minutes.* The thing can be the subject (*the tickets sold out*), or the seller can *sell out of* something (*We've sold out of bagels*). The adjective is *sold out* (*a sold-out show*); about a person, *sell out* means to give up your principles for money.
entries.pattern: tickets / a show + sell out; a store sells out of something
examples: Tickets for the concert **sold out** in less than ten minutes.
Sorry, we've **sold out of** the chocolate croissants — come back tomorrow.
The limited-edition sneakers **sold out** within an hour.

drill.sentence: Get to the farmers market early, because the strawberries usually {{sell out}} by nine.
drill.hint: are all bought, with none left (not *run out*)

entries.related: *run out of* — have none left, about the buyer or user; *be out of stock* — not available in a store; *fly off the shelves* — sell very quickly.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To slowly become less close as friends, partners or relatives, usually without a fight or a clear reason.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about friendships and marriages: *We just drifted apart.* It suggests no single cause and no blame, unlike *fall out* or *break up*. It has no object; the subject is both people (*we, they*), or one person *drifts apart from* another.
entries.pattern: we / they + drifted apart; drift apart from someone
examples: We were best friends in high school, but we **drifted apart** after college.
My parents didn't fight much; they just slowly **drifted apart**.
It's easy to **drift apart** from old friends when you move across the country.

drill.sentence: Once the kids were grown, Ana and her husband realized they had {{drifted apart}} and barely talked anymore.
drill.hint: slowly moved away from each other, like two boats with no one steering

entries.related: *grow apart* — very close; it suggests the two people changed in different directions; *lose touch* — stop being in contact; *fall out* — stop being friends after an argument.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To move, develop or make progress more slowly than other people or things, so that you are behind them.
entries.usage: Common in news, education and business: *lag behind other countries / the rest of the class / competitors*. It works with or without an object (*She lagged behind on the hike*). Unlike *fall behind*, which marks the moment you start to be behind, *lag behind* usually describes a gap that lasts.
entries.pattern: lag behind (+ others / competitors / the rest)
examples: Our youngest always **lags behind** on hikes because she stops to look at every bug.
Rural areas still **lag behind** cities when it comes to fast internet.
Wages have **lagged behind** rising rents for years.

drill.sentence: Our town still {{lags behind}} its neighbors on recycling; we only got curbside pickup last year.
drill.hint: is slower to make progress than (not *trails*)

entries.related: *fall behind* — start to be behind, often an event; *trail* — be behind in a competition; *catch up* — the opposite, reach the same level as others.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To do something important, such as getting married or buying a house, too quickly, without thinking about it enough.
entries.usage: Very common in advice, often negative: *Don't rush into anything*, *rush into marriage / a decision / buying a house*. It takes a noun or an *-ing* form after *into*. The passive *be rushed into* means that someone pressured you.
entries.pattern: rush into + a decision / marriage / -ing; be rushed into
examples: Don't **rush into** buying a house just because your friends are doing it.
They **rushed into** marriage after three months and divorced a year later.
I don't want to be **rushed into** a decision about the job offer.

drill.sentence: Take your time choosing a college; there's no reason to {{rush into}} anything.
drill.hint: decide too quickly on (not *jump into*)

entries.related: *jump into* — start something quickly and eagerly; *jump the gun* — act too early; *take your time* — the opposite, don't hurry.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To write something quickly, usually in a short form, so that you don't forget it.
entries.usage: Used for short notes such as numbers, ideas and addresses: *jot down a few notes / a phone number*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*jot it down*). It suggests speed and brevity, not careful writing.
entries.pattern: jot down + a number / a few notes / ideas; jot it down
examples: Let me **jot down** your number before I forget it.
I keep a notebook by the bed to **jot down** ideas in the middle of the night.
The officer **jotted down** a few notes while we described the accident.

drill.sentence: If you think of anything else we need from the store, just {{jot it down}} on the list on the fridge.
drill.hint: write it quickly, in a word or two

entries.related: *write down* — more general; *note down* — a bit more formal; *scribble* — write quickly and messily.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To see the difference between two or more people or things that look very similar.
entries.usage: Almost always used with *can't*, *hard to* or *how do you*: *I can't tell the twins apart.* The people or things being compared usually go in the middle, and a pronoun always does (*tell them apart*). For two separate items, the pattern is *tell A from B*.
entries.pattern: can't tell + them / the twins + apart; tell A from B
examples: The twins wear different colors so their teachers can **tell them apart**.
I honestly can't **tell** these two brands of olive oil **apart**.
It's surprisingly hard to **tell** real and fake designer bags **apart**.

drill.sentence: My two cats look so alike that only my daughter can {{tell them apart}}.
drill.hint: know which cat is which

mistake.wrong: They look so alike that I can't tell apart them.
mistake.right: They look so alike that I can't tell them apart.
mistake.why: With a pronoun object, the pronoun must come between *tell* and *apart*.

entries.related: *tell the difference between* — same idea, with *between*; *distinguish* — formal; *mix up* — the opposite, confuse one with the other.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To destroy a building, wall or other structure on purpose, because it is no longer wanted or safe.
entries.usage: Common in news about cities and homes: *tear down an old building / a wall / a house*. It is often passive (*The stadium was torn down in 2009*), and a pronoun goes in the middle (*tear it down*). The past forms are *tore* and *torn*.
entries.pattern: tear down + a building / a wall; be torn down
examples: They **tore down** the old movie theater and built a parking garage.
The house was **torn down** after the fire because it wasn't safe.
We want to **tear down** the wall between the kitchen and the dining room.

drill.sentence: The city plans to {{tear down}} the abandoned factory and turn the land into a park.
drill.hint: demolish — the usual American choice for an old building

entries.related: *knock down* — same meaning, a little more informal; *demolish* — formal; *put up* — the opposite, build.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To write a complete report, article or document based on notes, an investigation or an event.
entries.usage: Common at work, in science, journalism and police work: *write up the results / the minutes / a report*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*write it up*), and the noun *write-up* means a written report or review. It means turning rough material into a finished text, not just writing something down.
entries.pattern: write up + the results / a report / your notes; a write-up
examples: I took notes during the interview and **wrote them up** that evening.
She spent the summer **writing up** her research for her thesis.
The reporter **wrote up** the story in an hour so it could run in the morning edition.

drill.sentence: After the meeting, can you {{write up}} a short summary and send it to everyone?
drill.hint: turn your notes into a proper document (not *type up* or *put together*)

entries.related: *write down* — record something quickly; *draw up* — prepare a formal plan or contract; *type up* — make a typed copy of handwritten notes.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To choose one thing from several possibilities, often after thinking about it.
entries.usage: Common in news, reviews and slightly formal speech: *opt for the cheaper option / the train / a smaller wedding*. It sounds a little more formal than *choose* or *go for*. It takes a noun after *for*; with a verb, use *opt to* (*She opted to stay home*).
entries.pattern: opt for + a noun; opt to + verb
examples: Instead of a big wedding, they **opted for** a small ceremony at the beach.
More commuters are **opting for** bikes now that the city has more bike lanes.
I **opted for** the cheaper flight, even though it had a six-hour layover.

drill.sentence: Most of the class {{opted for}} the essay question instead of the multiple-choice section.
drill.hint: chose (not *went for* or *settled on*)

entries.related: *go for* — informal, choose; *settle on* — finally choose after a long time; *opt out* — choose not to take part.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To choose not to take part in something, or to leave a system or plan that you would otherwise be part of.
entries.usage: Common in official, business and online contexts: *opt out of emails / a retirement plan / data sharing / the class trip*. Use *of* before the thing you leave. The opposite is *opt in*, and the noun *opt-out* is common (*an opt-out form*).
entries.pattern: opt out of + emails / a plan / -ing
examples: You can **opt out of** the marketing emails by clicking the link at the bottom.
Several parents **opted out of** the field trip because of the cost.
Employees are enrolled automatically, but they can **opt out** at any time.

drill.sentence: If you don't want the company to share your data, you have to {{opt out}} in the app settings.
drill.hint: choose not to take part (not *unsubscribe*)

entries.related: *opt in* — the opposite, choose to take part; *drop out* — leave something before it ends; *sit out* — not take part in one activity or round.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To do something bad, extreme or unpleasant because nothing else has worked.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news: *resort to violence / threats / lying / begging*. The *to* is a preposition, so a verb after it takes *-ing* (*resort to borrowing*). It sounds critical or regretful; the related fixed phrase is *as a last resort*.
entries.pattern: resort to + a noun / -ing
examples: When the toddler wouldn't eat, we **resorted to** hiding vegetables in his pasta sauce.
The landlord **resorted to** threats when the tenants refused to move out.
I hate to **resort to** bribery, but I'll pay you twenty bucks to help me move.

drill.sentence: The two neighbors couldn't agree about the fence, so they finally {{resorted to}} suing each other.
drill.hint: did something extreme because nothing else worked (not *ended up* or *turned to*)

mistake.wrong: We had to resort to borrow money from my uncle.
mistake.right: We had to resort to borrowing money from my uncle.
mistake.why: *To* in *resort to* is a preposition, so it is followed by a noun or an *-ing* form.

entries.related: *turn to* — go to someone or something for help, neutral; *fall back on* — use a backup option; *stoop to* — do something morally low.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To demand something firmly, or to say firmly that you will do something, and not accept a refusal.
entries.usage: Common in polite situations and in complaints: *She insisted on paying*, *insist on a refund*. A verb after *on* takes *-ing* (*insist on going*), and another person can come before it (*insist on me coming*). With a full clause, use *insist that*, not *insist on that*.
entries.pattern: insist on + a noun / -ing; insist that + clause
examples: My grandfather **insists on** paying whenever we go out to eat.
The customer **insisted on** speaking to the manager.
I always **insist on** a written contract before I start a freelance job.

drill.sentence: I offered to drive her, but she {{insisted on}} taking the bus to the airport.
drill.hint: firmly wanted, and wouldn't change her mind

mistake.wrong: He insisted to pay for dinner.
mistake.right: He insisted on paying for dinner.
mistake.why: *Insist* is followed by *on* + *-ing* or by a *that*-clause, not by a *to*-infinitive.

entries.related: *demand* — ask firmly, often angrily; *be set on* — be determined to do something; *press for* — keep asking for something.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To say that you disagree with or oppose something, or to feel that it is wrong or unfair.
entries.usage: Common in neutral and formal contexts: *object to a plan / a decision / the noise*. The *to* is a preposition, so a verb takes *-ing* (*I object to being called that*). The verb is stressed on the second syllable, *ob-JECT*; the noun *OB-ject* is stressed on the first.
entries.pattern: object to + a noun / -ing
examples: Several neighbors **objected to** the plan to build a cell tower behind the school.
I **object to** being called "sweetie" by people I've never met.
My dad **objects to** paying for anything he can do himself, like haircuts.

drill.sentence: The defense attorney {{objected to}} the question, and the judge agreed.
drill.hint: formally protested against

mistake.wrong: Many residents object to pay higher parking fees.
mistake.right: Many residents object to paying higher parking fees.
mistake.why: *To* in *object to* is a preposition, so a verb after it takes the *-ing* form.

entries.related: *oppose* — be against, more formal; *protest* — show strong disagreement, often publicly; *mind* — dislike something mildly (*Do you mind if …?*).

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To think that something or someone is good, right or acceptable.
entries.usage: Common in talk about family, behavior and choices: *My parents didn't approve of him.* Use *of* for an opinion; *approve* without *of* means to accept something officially (*approve a budget*). It is often negative or in questions, and it can be used alone: *Do you approve?*
entries.pattern: approve of + someone / something / someone's -ing
examples: Her parents never **approved of** him, so they got married at city hall without telling anyone.
I don't **approve of** kids having phones in elementary school.
My grandmother doesn't **approve of** tattoos, so I wear long sleeves at family dinners.

drill.sentence: My boss doesn't {{approve of}} people eating lunch at their desks, but everyone does it anyway.
drill.hint: think it's acceptable (not *agree with*)

mistake.wrong: My parents don't approve my new boyfriend.
mistake.right: My parents don't approve of my new boyfriend.
mistake.why: For an opinion about someone, use *approve of*; *approve* + object means to accept something officially.

entries.related: *disapprove of* — the opposite; *agree with* — share an opinion, or think an action is right; *frown on* — disapprove, a little formal.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be made up of particular parts, things or members.
entries.usage: Neutral to formal, common in descriptions and reports: *The committee consists of nine members.* It is a state verb, so it is not used in the progressive or the passive (*is consisted of* is wrong). *Be made up of* and *be composed of* mean the same but are passive in form.
entries.pattern: X consists of + parts / members / items
examples: Breakfast at the hostel **consisted of** bread, jam and very weak coffee.
The committee **consists of** six parents and three teachers.
Each sample **consisted of** about two hundred cells from the same patient.

drill.sentence: My dad's idea of a vegetable garden {{consists of}} three tomato plants and a lot of weeds.
drill.hint: has as its only parts (not *is made up of* or *amounts to*)

mistake.wrong: The team is consisted of five engineers.
mistake.right: The team consists of five engineers.
mistake.why: *Consist of* is never passive; use the active form, or say *is made up of*.

entries.related: *be made up of* — same meaning, more common in speech; *comprise* — formal, the whole comprises the parts; *include* — contain as some of the parts, not all.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be one of the causes of something, often something bad, such as a problem, an illness or an accident.
entries.usage: Common in news, health and science: *contribute to the crash / stress / heart disease / the decline*. It suggests one cause among several, not the only one, and it is frequent with *factors* (*factors that contributed to the fire*). Americans stress the second syllable: *con-TRIB-ute*.
entries.pattern: X contributes to + a problem / an outcome; a contributing factor
examples: Lack of sleep can **contribute to** headaches and poor concentration.
Investigators say icy roads **contributed to** the crash on Route 9.
High rents have **contributed to** the closing of many small shops downtown.

drill.sentence: Cheap flights have {{contributed to}} overcrowding in some of Europe's most popular cities.
drill.hint: been one of the causes of (not *led to* or *added to*)

entries.related: *lead to* — cause, often as the main cause; *play a role in* — be one of several causes; *cause* — be the direct reason.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To take part in an activity, especially a serious, formal or illegal one.
entries.usage: Formal and common in news, law, research and official writing: *engage in conversation / research / criminal activity / risky behavior*. In everyday speech, *take part in* or simply *do* sounds more natural. The activity follows *in*, usually as a noun or an *-ing* form.
entries.pattern: engage in + an activity / behavior / -ing
examples: The company was fined for **engaging in** misleading advertising.
Teenagers who get enough sleep are less likely to **engage in** risky behavior.
We **engaged in** some polite small talk while we waited for the elevator.

drill.sentence: Students who {{engage in}} extracurricular activities tend to have better grades and attendance.
drill.hint: are actively involved in, formal (not *participate in* or *take part in*)

entries.related: *take part in* — neutral, more common in speech; *participate in* — formal, similar; *engage with* — interact actively with people or ideas.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To become actively involved with people or ideas, by paying attention to them, responding and taking them seriously.
entries.usage: Common in education, business and media: *engage with students / customers / the community / an argument / the material*. It suggests real interaction, not just being present. To *engage with* an idea means to think about it seriously instead of dismissing it.
entries.pattern: engage with + people / an idea / the material
examples: Good teachers find ways to get quiet students to **engage with** the material.
The new manager makes an effort to **engage with** customers instead of hiding in the office.
He didn't really **engage with** my argument; he just repeated his own point louder.

drill.sentence: The museum added hands-on exhibits so that kids could {{engage with}} the science instead of just reading signs.
drill.hint: really get involved with, not just look at (not *connect with* or *interact with*)

entries.related: *engage in* — take part in an activity; *interact with* — communicate or work together; *connect with* — form an emotional link.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be equal to a particular total, or to have the same effect or meaning as something else.
entries.usage: Used for totals (*The bill amounted to $300*) and, very often, for judgments: *That amounts to theft*, *His answer amounted to a no.* *Not amount to much* or *anything* means not to be important or successful. The object always follows *to*.
entries.pattern: X amounts to + a total / a judgment; not amount to much
examples: Our takeout orders **amount to** about four hundred dollars a month.
Asking me to work every weekend without extra pay **amounts to** a pay cut.
His apology **amounted to** little more than "sorry if you were offended."

drill.sentence: Copying someone else's homework and handing it in as your own {{amounts to}} cheating.
drill.hint: is in effect the same as (not *equals* or *counts as*)

entries.related: *add up to* — reach a total; *come to* — reach a total, about bills and prices; *be tantamount to* — formal, be as bad as.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To include something, such as a possible delay, cost or change, in your plans or calculations.
entries.usage: Common in planning, travel, budgets and instructions: *allow for traffic / delays / mistakes / shrinkage*. It means you plan with room for something that may happen. Don't confuse it with *allow* + object, which means to permit something.
entries.pattern: allow for + delays / traffic / extra costs
examples: Leave at seven to **allow for** traffic on the bridge.
Buy the jeans a little big to **allow for** shrinking in the wash.
Our budget **allows for** one dinner out a week, not three.

drill.sentence: When you book the connecting flight, {{allow for}} delays — the first flight is often late.
drill.hint: leave extra time in case of (not *plan for*, *account for* or *factor in*)

entries.related: *account for* — include in a calculation, or explain; *factor in* — include as one part of a decision; *plan for* — prepare for something that may happen.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To accept and follow a rule, law, agreement or decision, even if you do not like it.
entries.usage: Formal and common in contracts, official rules and news: *abide by the rules / the law / the terms / the court's decision*. It suggests obeying something you have agreed to or must accept. In everyday speech, *follow* or *stick to* sounds more natural.
entries.pattern: abide by + the rules / the law / a decision / the terms
examples: All players must **abide by** the league's rules on equipment.
Both sides agreed to **abide by** the judge's decision.
If you rent in this building, you have to **abide by** the no-pets policy.

drill.sentence: Guests who don't {{abide by}} the quiet hours after ten at night may be asked to leave the campground.
drill.hint: accept and follow, formal (not *observe* or *comply with*)

entries.related: *comply with* — obey a rule or request, formal; *stick to* — keep to a rule or plan, informal; *break* — the opposite, not follow a rule.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To obey a rule, law, standard or request, especially an official one.
entries.usage: Formal and very common in business, law and official letters: *comply with regulations / the law / safety standards / a request*. The noun is *compliance*. The rule always follows *with*; *comply the rules* is wrong.
entries.pattern: comply with + regulations / the law / standards / a request
examples: The factory was shut down because it didn't **comply with** safety standards.
Your carry-on bag must **comply with** the airline's size limits, or you'll pay a fee.
The app was updated to **comply with** new privacy laws in Europe.

drill.sentence: The landlord refused to {{comply with}} the city's order to fix the heating.
drill.hint: obey, formal (not *follow* or *abide by*)

mistake.wrong: All restaurants must comply the new health rules.
mistake.right: All restaurants must comply with the new health rules.
mistake.why: *Comply* takes no direct object; the rule always follows *with*.

entries.related: *abide by* — accept and follow, formal; *conform to* — meet a standard; *obey* — do what a person or law tells you.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To promise, or decide firmly, to give your time, energy or support to something.
entries.usage: Common in relationships, work and planning: *commit to a plan / a relationship / a date / doing something*. The *to* is a preposition, so a verb takes *-ing* (*commit to exercising daily*). It is often used without an object about people who avoid decisions: *He just won't commit.*
entries.pattern: commit to + a noun / -ing; commit yourself to
examples: Before you adopt a dog, make sure you can **commit to** walking it twice a day.
He likes her a lot, but he isn't ready to **commit to** a serious relationship.
We can't **commit to** a date for the reunion until we know who's coming.

drill.sentence: If you join the choir, you need to {{commit to}} every Tuesday rehearsal until the concert.
drill.hint: promise to attend (not *stick to*)

mistake.wrong: I've committed to run a marathon next spring.
mistake.right: I've committed to running a marathon next spring.
mistake.why: *To* in *commit to* is a preposition, so it is followed by a noun or an *-ing* form.

entries.related: *sign up for* — agree to join something; *dedicate yourself to* — give a lot of time to something; *back out of* — the opposite, withdraw from a commitment.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To think carefully and seriously about something, especially your past actions or experiences.
entries.usage: Common in education, interviews, speeches and personal writing: *reflect on the past / the year / your choices / what went wrong*. It is calmer and more serious than *think about*. *Reflect on* someone also means to give an impression of them: *This reflects badly on the school.*
entries.pattern: reflect on + the past / your choices / what happened
examples: At the end of each year, I like to **reflect on** what went well and what didn't.
After the accident, he had plenty of time in the hospital to **reflect on** his choices.
Teachers asked students to **reflect on** what they learned during the field trip.

drill.sentence: On the anniversary of her father's death, she always takes a quiet walk to {{reflect on}} his life.
drill.hint: think deeply about (not *dwell on* or *look back on*)

entries.related: *dwell on* — keep thinking about something bad; *look back on* — remember a past time; *mull over* — think about a decision for some time.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To explain something you have said in more detail.
entries.usage: Common in meetings, interviews and formal discussion, often as a polite request: *Could you elaborate on that?* The verb ends in a full *-ate* (*ih-LAB-uh-rayt*), unlike the adjective *elaborate* (*ih-LAB-er-it*). The topic follows *on*, but the verb also works alone: *Can you elaborate?*
entries.pattern: elaborate on + a point / the reasons / that
examples: Could you **elaborate on** what you mean by "a few changes"?
The police chief declined to **elaborate on** the reasons for the arrest.
In the interview, she **elaborated on** why she left her last job.

drill.sentence: The coach wouldn't {{elaborate on}} the injury, saying only that the player would miss "a few games."
drill.hint: explain in more detail (not *expand on* or *go into*)

entries.related: *expand on* — add more detail, very similar; *go into* — discuss in detail, less formal; *clarify* — make something clearer.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To suggest something in an indirect way, without saying it clearly.
entries.usage: Common in news, reviews and conversation: *hint at a sequel / changes / problems / retirement*. The subject can be a person or a thing (*The trailer hints at a darker story*). With a full clause, use *hint that* (*She hinted that she might quit*).
entries.pattern: hint at + a noun; hint that + clause
examples: The director **hinted at** a sequel in the final scene.
My boss has been **hinting at** layoffs for weeks without saying anything clear.
Dark clouds over the hills **hinted at** the storm that was coming.

drill.sentence: In her last interview, the singer {{hinted at}} retirement but refused to confirm it.
drill.hint: suggested indirectly (not *alluded to*)

entries.related: *allude to* — mention indirectly, formal; *imply* — suggest without saying directly; *drop a hint* — give a small sign on purpose.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To have the right to receive something, such as a discount, a benefit or a loan, or to take part in something, such as a competition.
entries.usage: Common in finance, public services, sports and shopping: *qualify for a loan / financial aid / free shipping / the finals*. It means you meet a set of official conditions. The thing you get follows *for*; *qualify as* means to count as something (*qualify as a small business*).
entries.pattern: qualify for + a discount / a loan / aid / the finals
examples: Orders over fifty dollars **qualify for** free shipping.
Our income is too high to **qualify for** financial aid.
She finished third and **qualified for** the national championships.

drill.sentence: Seniors over sixty-five {{qualify for}} a discount on bus passes in our city.
drill.hint: have the right to get (not *are eligible for* or *are entitled to*)

entries.related: *be eligible for* — same meaning, more formal; *be entitled to* — have a legal or official right to; *qualify as* — count as.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To consider something carefully, often for some time, before you make a decision.
entries.usage: Very common when you don't want to decide right away: *Let me think it over.* A pronoun must go in the middle (*think it over*), and a noun can go before or after *over*. It is polite and neutral, and often used to delay an answer to an offer.
entries.pattern: think it / things over; think over + an offer
examples: Thanks for the job offer — can I **think it over** for a day or two?
Take the weekend to **think things over** before you sign the lease.
He **thought over** his brother's offer carefully and decided to turn it down.

drill.sentence: I'm not saying no to the move. I just need some time to {{think it over}}.
drill.hint: consider it carefully before deciding — verb + *it* + particle (not *mull it over*)

entries.related: *sleep on it* — wait until tomorrow before you decide; *mull over* — think about something for a long time; *weigh the pros and cons* — compare the good and bad sides.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To interrupt someone while they are speaking, so that they cannot finish.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and in talk about meetings and interviews; it often sounds rude: *Stop cutting me off!* A pronoun must go in the middle (*cut me off*). The same verb also means to drive suddenly in front of another car, or to stop someone's supply of something.
entries.pattern: cut someone off (in the middle of a sentence)
examples: Every time I try to explain, you **cut me off**.
The host **cut the guest off** in the middle of his answer to go to a commercial.
Sorry, I didn't mean to **cut you off** — please finish your thought.

drill.sentence: She was halfway through her story when her husband {{cut her off}} to correct the date.
drill.hint: interrupted her (not *talked over her*)

entries.related: *interrupt* — more neutral; *talk over someone* — keep talking while they speak; *butt in* — informal, join a conversation rudely.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To leave a school, course, race or competition before you finish it.
entries.usage: Common with *college, high school, the race, the program*: *She dropped out of college to start a business.* Use *of* before the thing you leave. The noun *dropout* means a person who left school early, and it can sound negative.
entries.pattern: drop out of + college / school / the race
examples: He **dropped out of** college after a year to work in his family's restaurant.
Three runners **dropped out** of the marathon because of the heat.
If too many people **drop out**, the evening class will be canceled.

drill.sentence: My cousin {{dropped out of}} high school at sixteen but later got her diploma at night school.
drill.hint: left before finishing (not *quit*)

entries.related: *quit* — stop doing something, more general; *pull out of* — withdraw from a deal or event; *flunk out* — informal, be forced to leave school because of bad grades.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To begin your life, career or an activity in a particular way or position, especially one that later changes.
entries.usage: Common in stories about careers and change: *start out as a waiter / in sales / small*. It usually contrasts the beginning with what came later. It is followed by *as* + role, *in* + field, or an adjective (*It started out small*).
entries.pattern: start out as + role / in + field / + adjective
examples: She **started out** as a waitress and now owns three restaurants.
The company **started out** in a garage with just two employees.
We **started out** as roommates and ended up married.

drill.sentence: Lots of great musicians played for tips in subway stations when they were just {{starting out}}.
drill.hint: in the first years of their careers

entries.related: *start off* — begin an activity or event in a certain way; *get your start* — get your first chance in a career; *end up* — the other end of the story: finally be in a place or situation.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To have existed since a particular time in the past.
entries.usage: Common in history, travel and family talk: *date back to the 1800s / Roman times / my childhood*. It is a state verb, so the simple present is normal even for very old things (*The bridge dates back to 1720*). *Date from* means the same and is a bit more formal.
entries.pattern: X dates back to + a year / a period
examples: Our house **dates back to** the 1890s, so nothing in it is quite straight.
The town's Fourth of July parade **dates back** more than a hundred years.
Their friendship **dates back to** kindergarten.

drill.sentence: Some of the oak trees in this park {{date back to}} before the city was founded.
drill.hint: have existed since; the usual phrase for the age of buildings and objects

entries.related: *go back to* — same meaning, more informal; *date from* — a little more formal; *trace back to* — find the origin of something.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be going to happen in the future, especially something difficult or important.
entries.usage: Common in speeches, news and serious conversation: *the challenges that lie ahead*, *Hard times lie ahead.* It is often used in a relative clause (*what lies ahead*), and the past form is *lay ahead*. It sounds a little serious or dramatic, so in casual talk people often say *what's coming* instead.
entries.pattern: what lies ahead; the challenges that lie ahead (of us)
examples: Nobody knows what **lies ahead**, so enjoy today.
The team knows a difficult season **lies ahead** after losing its best player.
With a new baby, we knew that many sleepless nights **lay ahead**.

drill.sentence: The hardest part of the climb {{lies ahead}}, so rest while you can.
drill.hint: is still to come (not *awaits*)

entries.related: *be in store* — be going to happen to someone; *await* — formal, be waiting for someone; *loom* — seem close and threatening.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To start doing an activity with a lot of energy and enthusiasm, giving it most of your time and attention.
entries.usage: Common in talk about work, hobbies and difficult times: *throw yourself into your work / a project / training*. The reflexive pronoun changes with the subject (*she threw herself into*, *we threw ourselves into*). It often suggests using activity to forget something painful.
entries.pattern: throw + myself / herself / ourselves … + into + an activity
examples: After the divorce, she **threw herself into** her work and got promoted twice.
We **threw ourselves into** fixing up the old house the summer we bought it.
If you're nervous about the new school, **throw yourself into** a club or a sport.

drill.sentence: When his dog died, my son {{threw himself into}} soccer practice and barely talked about it.
drill.hint: put all his energy into (not *dove into*)

entries.related: *dive into* — start something quickly and eagerly; *immerse yourself in* — become completely involved in something; *bury yourself in* — work hard to avoid other things.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To return to a topic or question later in a discussion or a piece of work.
entries.usage: Very common in meetings, classes and presentations: *Let's come back to that later*, *I'll come back to your question.* It is a polite way to postpone a topic without ignoring it. The topic follows *to*, often as *that* or *it*.
entries.pattern: come back to + that / it / a question (later)
examples: Good question — let me **come back to** that after I finish this slide.
We can't agree on a name for the puppy, so let's **come back to** it tomorrow.
If you get stuck on a crossword clue, skip it and **come back to** it later.

drill.sentence: Can we {{come back to}} the guest list later? Right now I just want to pick a date for the wedding.
drill.hint: postpone, then return to (not *revisit*)

entries.related: *get back to* — return to a topic, or reply to someone later; *revisit* — look at a topic or decision again; *table* — American, postpone discussion of something.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To reach the same decision or opinion as other people, usually after discussing it.
entries.usage: Common in planning and negotiation: *agree on a price / a date / a plan / the details*. The subject is usually plural (*We agreed on a price*), or one person agrees on something *with* another. Compare *agree with* (share someone's opinion) and *agree to* (accept a proposal).
entries.pattern: agree on + a price / a date / a plan / what to do
examples: After an hour of arguing, we finally **agreed on** a name for the dog.
The two sides couldn't **agree on** a price, so the sale fell through.
Doctors don't all **agree on** the best treatment for back pain.

drill.sentence: My roommates and I can never {{agree on}} what to watch, so we take turns choosing.
drill.hint: reach the same choice, as a group (not *settle on* or *decide on*)

mistake.wrong: We couldn't agree with a date for the party.
mistake.right: We couldn't agree on a date for the party.
mistake.why: *Agree on* means to decide something together; *agree with* means to share someone's opinion.

entries.related: *agree with* — share an opinion; *agree to* — accept a request or proposal; *settle on* — finally choose after discussion.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To choose something after thinking about the different options.
entries.usage: Common in everyday choices: *decide on a name / a color / a restaurant / a date*. It takes a noun after *on* and focuses on the final choice; with a verb, use *decide to* (*decide to stay*). *Have you decided on …?* is a common question.
entries.pattern: decide on + a noun; decide to + verb
examples: We still haven't **decided on** a color for the baby's room.
After visiting five schools, they **decided on** the one closest to home.
Have you **decided on** a place for the wedding yet?

drill.sentence: It took my dad two hours at the dealership to {{decide on}} a car, and he ended up with the first one he'd looked at.
drill.hint: make a final choice of (not *settle on* or *pick out*)

entries.related: *settle on* — finally choose, often after a long time; *opt for* — choose, a little formal; *go with* — informal, choose.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To end a relationship, an engagement, talks or contact with someone, often suddenly.
entries.usage: Common with *an engagement, a relationship, talks, negotiations, contact*: *She broke off the engagement.* A pronoun goes in the middle (*break it off*), and *break it off with someone* is a common way to say you ended a romance. It sounds sudden and final.
entries.pattern: break off + an engagement / talks / contact; break it off (with someone)
examples: She **broke off** the engagement two months before the wedding.
The union **broke off** talks with the company after the latest offer.
He decided to **break it off** with her before he moved to London.

drill.sentence: After years of arguing about money, he {{broke off}} all contact with his brother.
drill.hint: ended suddenly (not *cut off*)

entries.related: *break up* — end a romantic relationship; *call off* — cancel an event or a plan; *cut off* — stop contact or a supply.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To start ringing or making a loud noise suddenly, used about alarms and phones; or to explode, used about bombs and fireworks.
entries.usage: Common with *my alarm, the fire alarm, the smoke detector, a car alarm, a phone* and *a bomb*: *My alarm didn't go off.* It is intransitive. In British English, food that *goes off* has gone bad; Americans say *go bad* or *spoil*.
entries.pattern: an alarm / a phone / a bomb + goes off
examples: My alarm didn't **go off**, so I was late for my first day.
The smoke detector **goes off** every time I make toast.
A firework **went off** too close to the crowd, and two people were hurt.

drill.sentence: The whole theater turned around when a phone {{went off}} during the quietest scene of the play.
drill.hint: suddenly started ringing

entries.related: *ring* — make the sound of a bell or phone; *explode* — burst violently; *set off* — make an alarm or a bomb start.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To study a subject as your main field at a college or university.
entries.usage: Standard in American higher education: *major in biology / economics / English*. The noun is also very common (*What's your major?*, *She's a history major*), and *minor in* names a second, smaller field. British English usually says *study* a subject or *do a degree in* it.
entries.pattern: major in + a subject; be a + subject + major
examples: I **majored in** history, but I ended up working in marketing.
What are you planning to **major in**? You don't have to decide yet.
She **majored in** chemistry and then went to medical school.

drill.sentence: My parents wanted me to {{major in}} accounting, but I switched to music in my second year.
drill.hint: study as my main college subject

entries.related: *minor in* — study a second, smaller subject; *specialize in* — focus on one area, often later in a career; *graduate with a degree in* — finish college in a subject.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To be the period of time or the events just before something important, often causing it.
entries.usage: Very common as *the days / weeks leading up to* + an event, and in *the events that led up to the accident*. It describes the time before an event or the steps that caused it. The noun *lead-up* is common too (*in the lead-up to the holidays*).
entries.pattern: the days / weeks leading up to + an event; what led up to X
examples: What **led up to** your decision to leave the band?
Police are still trying to piece together the events that **led up to** the crash.
In the days **leading up to** the wedding, my mom made about fifty lists.

drill.sentence: Tell me exactly what happened in the hours {{leading up to}} the fight.
drill.hint: coming just before and building toward (not *before*)

entries.related: *lead to* — cause directly; *build up to* — gradually prepare for something; *in the run-up to* — in the period before an event.

entries.label: phrasal verb (separable)
entries.meaning: To force someone to leave a place, a group, a school or a home.
entries.usage: Informal and very common: *get kicked out of school / a bar / the house*. A pronoun goes in the middle (*kick him out*), and the passive with *get* is especially frequent. More formal words are *expel* for schools and *evict* for housing.
entries.pattern: kick someone out (of + a place); get kicked out (of …)
examples: He got **kicked out** of the bar for starting a fight.
Her parents **kicked her out** when she was seventeen, and she moved in with her aunt.
The band **kicked out** their drummer after he missed three shows.

drill.sentence: The security guard {{kicked us out}} of the mall because we were skateboarding near the fountain.
drill.hint: made us leave (not *threw us out*)

entries.related: *throw out* — same meaning, informal; *expel* — formal, force a student to leave a school; *evict* — legally force a tenant to leave.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To defend yourself or resist when someone attacks, criticizes or threatens you.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports and personal stories: *fight back against critics / an attacker*. It has no object; use *against* for the attacker. In sports it also means to recover after losing, and *fight back tears* means to try hard not to cry.
entries.pattern: fight back (against + someone / something)
examples: When the man grabbed her bag, she **fought back** and screamed for help.
The small bookstore is **fighting back** against online giants with author events and a café.
Down by two goals at halftime, the team **fought back** to win three to two.

drill.sentence: Our self-defense class teaches you how to {{fight back}} if someone grabs you from behind.
drill.hint: resist an attacker physically (not *defend yourself*)

entries.related: *hit back* — respond strongly to an attack or criticism; *stand up to* — resist someone more powerful; *retaliate* — formal, attack in return.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To become more intense, active, exciting or competitive.
entries.usage: Common in sports, news and business: *the race / the competition / the debate / the rivalry is heating up*. In this sense it is often in the progressive and has no object. Literally, *heat up* means to become hot or to make food hot (*heat up the leftovers*).
entries.pattern: the race / competition / argument + is heating up
examples: The race for first place is really **heating up** with three games left.
Things started to **heat up** when my brother brought up the inheritance.
Competition between food delivery apps has **heated up** in the past year.

drill.sentence: The housing market usually {{heats up}} in the spring, when families want to move before the new school year.
drill.hint: gets busier and more competitive (not *picks up* or *warms up*)

entries.related: *pick up* — become busier or stronger; *intensify* — formal; *cool off* — the opposite, become calmer or less active.
